title: My Cousin Laughed Over a Chipped Dish, Then I Opened Aunt Inez's Box

blocks.text: "Take the candy dish and quit whining," my cousin Maxine said after Aunt Inez's funeral.

We were standing in Aunt Inez's kitchen while the rest of the family was still out by the driveway. Maxine already had the house keys clipped to her purse. By that point, everyone knew how the paperwork had been set up. Maxine got the three-bedroom brick house, the silver Buick in the carport, and $96,000 in savings.
I got a chipped glass candy dish that had sat beside Aunt Inez's kitchen wall phone for 28 years.
I wasn't even asking for money. I had only asked if I could have the ceramic mixing bowl my grandmother used to make biscuits in, or one of Inez's Sunday brooches. Maxine wouldn't hear of it.
She picked the candy dish off the little shelf under the phone, held it out by the rim, and laughed.
"She knew what you were worth," Maxine said.

I didn't argue with her. I was 61 years old, my feet hurt from standing at the cemetery in cheap black flats, and I knew better than to start a yelling match in a dead woman's kitchen. That was my problem with Maxine my whole life. I always backed down just to keep things quiet.
I didn't have a box, so I slipped the candy dish into a yellow Dollar General bag I'd left on my passenger seat and carried it out to my car.
The drive back to my apartment took forty minutes. By the time I got inside and set my purse on the counter, my thumb was throbbing.
When I reached into the Dollar General bag to pull the dish out, the chipped spot along the glass rim sliced right across the pad of my right thumb.
"Great," I muttered, grabbing a blue dish towel off the oven handle.

I pressed the towel hard against the cut and turned the candy dish upside down on the kitchen table to see how bad the chip was. That was when I noticed the green felt glued to the bottom. One corner had peeled loose from years of sitting near the kitchen sink. Something stiff was wedged underneath it.
I held the dish steady with my left hand, still wrapped in the towel, and peeled the felt back the rest of the way.
Taped flat against the glass with yellowed Scotch tape was a small brass key and a folded slip of paper.
I pulled the tape loose and smoothed the paper out on the table with my good hand.

It was a bank receipt from Citizens State Bank over in Millbrook, the town where Aunt Inez had lived since 1978. It was for a safe-deposit box renewal. $11 every January. There were three more thin receipts tucked inside the fold, all for $11, all paid in January.
I sat down at the table and stared at that flat key.

For 28 years, that dish had sat right under Aunt Inez's phone. I remembered the day she bought it at a church rummage sale after my mother passed away. Every Sunday night when I called to check on her, I could hear the glass lid clink while she fished out a peppermint before she talked.

Then something else came back to me. Six years ago, right after Inez had her mild stroke, she asked me to drive her to Citizens State Bank on a Tuesday afternoon. She had me sign a small yellow card at the counter.
She told me it was just in case she ever broke a hip and needed me to fetch her house deed. I had signed it without even reading the fine print and forgot all about it.
My thumb was still stinging, and a drop of blood had soaked through the blue towel. I wrapped the key and the $11 receipt in a clean napkin and dropped them into the zippered pocket of my purse.
I didn't go to the bank the next morning.

I work as a receptionist at a dental clinic, and I'd already taken two unpaid days off for the viewing and the funeral. On top of that, I spent the next two weeks talking myself out of it. I kept thinking the box probably held old tax returns or cemetery plots, and that going down to Millbrook would only stir up trouble with Maxine.
Maxine made sure to remind me she was in charge.

She texted me twice that first week. The first text said she was having the locks changed on Inez's house on Thursday. The second one asked if I wanted to buy Inez's old dining chairs for $150 before she put them on Facebook Marketplace. I didn't text her back.

Then the July heatwave hit. Three straight days near 98 degrees, with the air conditioning in my old Honda blowing warm air every time I stopped at a red light. On Friday, the clinic closed early for a staff training I didn't have to attend. I looked at my purse sitting on the chair, thought about Maxine laughing in that kitchen, and got in the car.
By the time I reached Millbrook, my blouse was stuck to my back. The lobby of Citizens State Bank felt like a refrigerator.
I walked up to the counter where a gray-haired woman in a navy cardigan was sorting deposit slips.
I laid my driver's license, the January receipt, and the flat key on the marble counter.
"I'm Carol Mercer," I said. "My aunt, Inez Mercer, passed away last month. I think my name might be on this box."
The woman looked at my license, then stepped over to a metal filing cabinet and pulled out a yellow card. She studied it for a second, looked back at me, and nodded.
"Yes, ma'am. You're listed as a co-lessee," she said. "Come on back with me."
She led me through a heavy steel door into the vault room and unlocked a tall bank of gray drawers. She slid one narrow metal box out and set it in my hands.
On the front of the box, stuck right above the handle, was a strip of white masking tape.
Written on it in Aunt Inez's neat, slanted cursive was my birth date: 10/14/64.
The teller showed me into a tiny privacy booth with a wooden table and pulled the door shut behind her.
My hands were shaking a little as I fitted the flat key into the lock and lifted the lid.

Inside, there wasn't any cash. There was a thick manila envelope with my name written across the front, a folded blue-and-white policy folder from Union Fidelity Life, and a small dark velvet pouch tied with a gold string.
I opened the manila envelope first. Inside was a two-page letter on lined notebook paper, dated two years back.
"Dear Carol," it started. "If you are reading this, you found the key I taped under the peppermint dish.
I knew Maxine would never hand you anything out of my jewelry box, and I knew if I left you a dime in the will, she would drag you into probate court until there wasn't anything left."
I had to stop for a second and swallow hard.

In the next paragraph, Inez wrote that after her second fall, Maxine had started coming over every other day, complaining about how tired she was and how much gas it cost to run Inez to the grocery store. Maxine had pressured her to add her name to the checking and savings accounts, and had hinted more than once that if Inez didn't sign the house over, Maxine wouldn't have time to help anymore. Inez wrote that she was too tired to fight her, so she let Maxine have the house, the Buick, and the $96,000 in savings.
"She thinks she got everything," Inez wrote.
"She never knew about this box, and she never knew about the policy I kept paid up from your uncle's union."
I set the letter down and opened the Union Fidelity Life folder.
It was a paid-up whole life insurance policy for $38,000. On the beneficiary line, typed clearly in black ink, was my full name. Not the estate. Not Maxine. Just me.

Then I untied the velvet pouch and tipped it into my palm. Out slid my grandmother's round gold locket, the one with the tiny black-and-white picture of my mother inside. The one Maxine had told me Aunt Inez must have lost years ago.
I sat in that cool little booth for ten minutes, reading the letter one more time. Maxine had spent three weeks bragging about the house and the Buick. She had no idea this box existed.
On Monday morning, I called Union Fidelity Life from my car during my lunch break.

The woman on the phone walked me through the claim form. Because I was the named beneficiary, the policy didn't go through Aunt Inez's estate at all. All they needed was the signed claim form, a copy of my ID, and a certified death certificate. I drove to the county clerk's office after work, paid $15 for a certified copy, and mailed the whole packet by certified mail the next afternoon.
For two weeks, I didn't hear a word from Maxine, and I didn't call her.
Then on a Thursday evening, my phone rang three times in a row. On the third ring, I answered.
"Where is it?" Maxine snapped before I even said hello.
"The gold locket," she said, her voice tight and shrill. "And whatever else you took out of Inez's desk.

I found an old bank receipt stuck behind the radiator when I was cleaning out the office. I went down to Citizens State Bank today and they told me there was a surviving co-owner on the box, and they wouldn't even let me look inside."
"I didn't take anything out of the desk," I said, keeping my voice flat. "I haven't set foot in that house since the funeral."
"Don't lie to me, Carol. You took that candy dish and you went straight to the bank."
